text.p: Trying to keep the latest Mideast crisis from derailing peace efforts, President Bill Clinton on Tuesday turns to personal diplomacy at an emergency summit called to defuse tensions between Israelis and Palestinians.

Clinton, who held late night talks with King Hussein of Jordan on Monday in the White House, was slated to confer separately on Tuesday with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat, who arrived in Washington about 5 a.m. EDT (0900 GMT), only hours before the talks were to begin.
Those morning talks were to set the stage for face-to-face sessions involving Netanyahu and Arafat, along with Clinton and King Hussein, on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Clinton and King Hussein huddled in the private residence of the White House for 45 minutes on salvaging the fragile peace process. Other participants included Vice President Al Gore and Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti.
"They discussed ways in which they could ... get the peace process back on track," said White House spokesman David Johnson.

U.S. officials sought to play down the chances for a dramatic breakthrough at the summit -- stressing instead that Clinton wanted to defuse tensions enough to nurture the search for a solution to the latest crisis.

Fifty-seven Palestinians and 14 Israelis were killed in five days of clashes on the West Bank and Gaza after Israel opened a pedestrian tunnelto archaeological sites near Jerusalem's Temple Mount, sacred to both Judaism and Islam.

"It's clear to me that the Middle East peace process is in a state of crisis," said Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who has devoted much of his energies to trying to end the region's ancient strife.

Christopher sought to lower expections for the summit, telling reporters candidly: "I think we ought to recognise the limitations. The parties are quite estranged and raw because of the violence and killings."
He said the objective of the summit was to convince the parties "to talk together again" and "find the basis for resuming negotiations" on stalled peace efforts.

Officials said there would be a news blackout during the summit. A U.S. official said the meetings would take place under "Dayton rules" -- a reference to the intensive closed-door U.S.-sponsored negotiations in Dayton, Ohio, that led to last year's Bosnian peace accord.
"The idea is for there to be no statements for 24 hours until the conclusion of the summit," said an Israeli official travelling with Netanyahu.

The summit was taking place not only against a backdrop of a sudden resumption of Israeli-Palestinian violence but in the midst of the U.S. election campaign, with Clinton under challenge by Republican Bob Dole in the Nov. 5 balloting.

Dole issued a statement saying that "American strategy for this meeting ... must be clear and decisive. We must demand an unconditional end to the violence. Our friend Israel must not be asked to make concessions as a means of restoring order."
Although the Republican challenger's statement was clearly in support of Israel, most public opinion polls showed Jewish-American voters favoured Clinton in the election.

One of the highlights of Clinton's presidency was his shepherding of Arafat and the late Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin into an "historic handshake" at 1993 White House ceremonies in which Israel and the Palestinians signed a peace accord designed to end a long and bloody feud.
Clinton, however, favoured former Prime Minister Shimon Peres in Israel's May elections -- leaving him with limited influence in his dealings with Netanyahu.
